samples.summary: New SSRF guard is bypassable by an HTTP redirect — `fetch` follows redirects by default and the allow-list is only checked on the initial URL
samples.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl(resolved, opts.serverBase)` runs once, before `await fetchImpl(resolved)` (image-fetcher.ts:151-152). Node/undici `fetch` defaults to `redirect: 'follow'` and does not re-invoke any caller-side check on the redirect target. Attack: a workspace member (or an agent-generated doc) sets an image inline `src` to `https://attacker.example/x.png`; the guard sees a public https host and allows it; the attacker's server answers `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`. `wafflebase docs export` / `slides export` running on an operator's cloud instance then GETs the metadata endpoint and embeds the response bytes into the exported PDF/DOCX/PPTX. The doc comment enumerates the residual gap as only "a public hostname that resolves to a private address" (line 107-109) — redirects are not mentioned and not handled, so the guard reads as covering a case it does not. Fix would be `redirect: 'manual'` plus re-running `assertFetchableImageUrl` on each `Location`.

samples.summary: `isPrivateHost` loopback check is bypassed by a trailing-dot FQDN (`localhost.`), and by any private-network DNS name
samples.evidence: `LOOPBACK_HOSTS` is an exact-match set (`localhost`, ``, `[::1]`, `::1`) plus a `.localhost` suffix test (image-fetcher.ts:38,47). The WHATWG URL parser does not strip a trailing dot from a *domain* host (it only does so in the IPv4 parser when the host ends in a number), so `new URL('http://localhost./x').hostname === 'localhost.'` — which matches neither the set nor `.localhost`, is not an IPv4/IPv6 literal, and therefore falls through to `return false` (line 65) and is fetched. The OS resolver treats `localhost.` as the same name. Same shape for an attacker-chosen internal name (`metadata.google.internal`, an intranet host) — the comment at line 107 acknowledges DNS-resolved names, but a bare `localhost.` bypass of an explicitly enumerated loopback check is a hole in the check itself, not in DNS.

samples.summary: Frontend `seg()` rule is applied only to `documents.ts`; every other API module still interpolates route-param ids raw into session-carrying URLs
samples.evidence: The change adds `packages/frontend/src/api/url.ts` and applies `seg()` in `documents.ts` only. Unencoded interpolation of ids that reach the browser from the URL bar remains at, among others: `api/workspaces.ts:184,196,212` (`${BASE}/${workspaceId}/api-keys`, POST/DELETE), `:102` (`members/${userId}`), `:143` (`invites/${inviteId}`), `api/folders.ts:10,24,42,64,82`, `api/share-links.ts:60,78,89,102`, `api/datasources.ts:45,65,78,90,104`, `api/analytics.ts:127`, `api/files.ts:22`, `app/spreadsheet/image-upload.ts:36`. Those ids are route params: `app/workspaces/workspace-settings.tsx:51` and `workspace-datasources.tsx:13` read `workspaceId` from `useParams`, `app/shared/shared-document.tsx:899` reads `token`. react-router percent-decodes params, so a crafted link such as `/workspaces/..%2F..%2Fauth%2Flogout/settings` makes `fetchWithAuth` issue the request against an endpoint the caller never named, with the victim's session attached (`fetch` resolves `..` per WHATWG). An added-but-partial gate reads as covered: the design doc it ships with states the rule is 'not CLI-only' while only the document routes actually enforce it.
searchedFor: grep for ${BASE}/${id} style interpolation in frontend/src/api
grep useParams call sites feeding workspaceId/token

samples.summary: `assertNoDotSegments` only rejects literal `.`/`..`, not the percent-encoded dot-segment spellings the URL parser also resolves
samples.evidence: The backstop compares each segment against the two literal strings (dry-run.ts:47-51). Per the WHATWG URL spec a 'double-dot path segment' is also `.%2e`, `%2e.` and `%2e%2e` (ASCII case-insensitive), and a single-dot segment is also `%2e`; the parser resolves all of them. A raw path reaching `printDryRun` whose id is spelled `%2e%2e` therefore passes the guard and prints a URL that walks out of `/api/v1/workspaces/<ws>` once an agent copies and runs it — the exact output the doc comment says the guard exists to prevent. `seg()` itself is safe (it escapes `%`), so this only weakens the documented backstop for a future/forgetful caller, not today's call sites.

samples.summary: Private-address list omits several non-public IPv4/IPv6 ranges (192.0.0.0/24, 198.18.0.0/15, multicast/reserved 224.0.0.0/3, IPv4-compatible and NAT64 IPv6)
samples.evidence: `isPrivateHost` (lines 52-65) covers 0/8, 10/8, 127/8, 169.254/16, 172.16-31, 192.168/16 and 100.64/10, and IPv6 `::`, `::1`, fc00::/7, fe80::/10. Not covered: 192.0.0.0/24 (IETF protocol assignments, includes some service addresses), 198.18.0.0/15 (benchmarking), 224.0.0.0/4 multicast, 240.0.0.0/4 and 255.255.255.255, IPv4-compatible IPv6 (`::7f00:1`, which `unwrapIpv4Mapped` does not fold because it requires the `::ffff:` prefix), and NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96` which some networks route to internal IPv4. Each is a residual, lower-value path for the same image-`src`-driven SSRF the guard is meant to close.

samples.summary: Upstream-controlled error text is printed into an agent's stderr with only length bounds — no control-character or instruction-content neutralisation
samples.evidence: `forwardUpstreamError` / `upstreamErrorJson` print `safeEnvelope(res.data, res.status)`, which keeps the upstream `code` (80 chars), `message` (500 chars) and *arbitrary sibling fields* of `res.data` while the serialised body stays under 4 KB (formatter.ts:158-171, 224-230, 249-250). The only content filter is `startsWith('<')` for HTML. A hostile or compromised backend (or a proxy on the path, since plain `http://` servers are allowed via `--server`) can therefore place up to ~4 KB of chosen prose — including terminal escape sequences and text shaped as instructions — directly into the stderr an AI agent reads and acts on. `JSON.stringify` escapes control characters, which limits the terminal-escape angle, so this is hardening rather than an exploit; worth noting because the CLI's stated consumer is an agent.

verdict.reason: The code is exactly as the finding describes. In packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts, assertFetchableImageUrl(resolved, opts.serverBase) runs once at line 151, then line 152 calls `await fetchImpl(resolved)` with no options object — so Node/undici's default `redirect: 'follow'` applies and the scheme allow-list (line 35/121-125) and private-address blocklist (isPrivateHost, lines 45-66, incl. 169.254/16 at line 55) are never re-applied to the redirect target. A grep for redirect/setGlobalDispatcher/undici across packages/cli finds no manual-redirect handling or dispatcher-level restriction, so nothing elsewhere guards it. The path is reachable from real commands: docs.ts:261-263 (`docs export`) and slides.ts:209 (`slides export`) construct the fetcher over document image `src` values, which are attacker-influenceable content, and the fetched bytes are embedded in the exported PDF/DOCX/PPTX. Attack chain: attacker-controlled `src` https://attacker/x.png passes the guard (public https host), attacker replies 302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/, the CLI running on a cloud instance follows it and embeds credentials into the export. This is SSRF, explicitly in the Security lane, and it is an added-but-bypassable gate whose doc comment (lines 107-109) enumerates a different residual gap and so reads as covering a case it does not.

finding.summary: `isPrivateHost` loopback check is bypassed by a trailing-dot FQDN (`localhost.`), and by any private-network DNS name
finding.evidence: `LOOPBACK_HOSTS` is an exact-match set (`localhost`, ``, `[::1]`, `::1`) plus a `.localhost` suffix test (image-fetcher.ts:38,47). The WHATWG URL parser does not strip a trailing dot from a *domain* host (it only does so in the IPv4 parser when the host ends in a number), so `new URL('http://localhost./x').hostname === 'localhost.'` — which matches neither the set nor `.localhost`, is not an IPv4/IPv6 literal, and therefore falls through to `return false` (line 65) and is fetched. The OS resolver treats `localhost.` as the same name. Same shape for an attacker-chosen internal name (`metadata.google.internal`, an intranet host) — the comment at line 107 acknowledges DNS-resolved names, but a bare `localhost.` bypass of an explicitly enumerated loopback check is a hole in the check itself, not in DNS.

verdict.reason: The claimed code is present exactly as described. LOOPBACK_HOSTS (image-fetcher.ts:38) is an exact-match set and the only fuzzy test is `host.endsWith('.localhost')` (line 47); normalization at line 46 lowercases and strips brackets only, never a trailing dot. A host of `localhost.` therefore matches neither, fails the IPv4 regex (line 49) and the IPv6 literal tests (lines 62-64), and falls through to `return false` at line 65 — classified public. WHATWG URL preserves the trailing dot for a domain-form host (the IPv4 parser is only entered when the host ends in a number), so `url.hostname` at line 128 is `localhost.`, which the OS resolver maps to 127.0.0.1. The gate at lines 128-132 is the sole address check for http/https, and it is reachable with attacker-influenced document image `src` via createImageFetcher -> assertFetchableImageUrl (line 151) from packages/cli/src/commands/docs.ts:261 and packages/cli/src/commands/slides.ts:209. Grep shows isPrivateHost/LOOPBACK_HOSTS appear nowhere else in packages/ (other hits are node_modules and prior review artifacts), so no upstream guard normalizes the hostname or makes this unreachable. SSRF is explicitly in the Security lane; the docstring at lines 107-109 waives only public DNS names resolving privately, not a literal bypass of the enumerated loopback set, so the trailing-dot hole is not out of scope. No named refutation ground applies.

verdict.reason: Verified independently. `seg()` exists at packages/frontend/src/api/url.ts:18-23 but a repo-wide grep for `seg(` matches only url.ts and api/documents.ts, so the encoding rule covers document routes alone. The cited raw interpolations are real: workspaces.ts:102 (`members/${userId}`), :143 (`invites/${inviteId}`), :184/:196/:212 (`api-keys`), plus :48,:75,:88,:115,:130,:156,:227,:272,:291,:304,:316,:339; folders.ts:10,24,42,64,82; share-links.ts:60,78,89,102. The ids are attacker-influenceable route params: workspace-settings.tsx:51 pulls `workspaceId` from useParams and feeds it unvalidated into fetchWorkspace(:71), fetchInvites(:93), revokeInvite(:122), removeMember(:133), fetchApiKeys(:145), revokeApiKey(:163), deleteWorkspace(:174); same pattern in workspace-datasources.tsx:13, workspace-analytics.tsx:29, shared-document.tsx:899. No guard exists downstream: auth.ts:136-144 fetchWithAuth passes `input` directly to `fetch` and adds `credentials: "include"`, performing no validation or encoding. A crafted link therefore issues credentialed same-origin requests (including DELETE/POST) against an endpoint the caller never named. This is unsafe input handling / path traversal on a session-carrying request, in the security lane, and the partially-applied rule matches the rubric's "added-but-bypassable gate reads as covered" case. No refutation ground applies.
